messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: positive transformation
parts:
I think this came up before, but I can't remember what was said. For a transformation of an unbounded parameter (x) to a positive parameter (y), we are using y = exp(x). Would it be better to do something like y = 0.5 * (sqrt(x^2 + 4) + x) whose inverse is x = y - 1 / y? This transformation does not overflow / underflow as rapidly as the exponential one. You can roundtrip negative 1 million and get back -999992.4 and can roundtrip pretty much any big positive number. There could be some numerical difficulties if a user initializes y to a really small number like 1e-9, but that seems like a lesser problem.

Ben

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] positive transformation
parts:
The cusp in the Jacobian at y = 0 will cause all kinds of problems for HMC.
But in general the pathological behavior for small x is not necessarily any
better than the overflow for exp, so which is better depends on the context.
Given the cusp in this one, though, I would recommend exp with an effort
to standardize the model as much as possible.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] positive transformation
parts:
One thing I've wondered about is the non-linearity of
the transform and how they work in different parts of the
space. For instance, with y = exp(x) as the inverse
transform, you get really big gradients when x is big,
whereas the approach Ben suggests will be much more gradual.

Since we take fixed step sizes and use a fixed mass matrix, I'd
think the non-linearities would make a big difference.

It would be easy enough to code this up yourself and try
it by transforming and unconstrained parameter and applying
the log Jacobian adjustment.

- Bob

messages.author: 49e107cb0f8a3d27
messages.subject: Re: positive transformation
parts:
On Tuesday, February 9, 2016 at 12:38:55 AM UTC-5, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> I think this came up before, but I can't remember what was said. For a transformation of an unbounded parameter (x) to a positive parameter (y), we are using y = exp(x). Would it be better to do something like y = 0.5 * (sqrt(x^2 + 4) + x) whose inverse is x = y - 1 / y? This transformation does not overflow / underflow as rapidly as the exponential one. You can roundtrip negative 1 million and get back -999992.4 and can roundtrip pretty much any big positive number. There could be some numerical difficulties if a user initializes y to a really small number like 1e-9, but that seems like a lesser problem.
>
> Ben
>

This is a really cool idea. I mentioned this to Rajesh Ranganath, and we went into discussion about this vs log(1 + exp(x)), and generally what are the criteria that we desire from transformations. The latter is more popular in optimization and the machine learning literature. log( 1+ exp(x) ) and its inverse can loop back and forth for very large positive numbers but can only go down to around -740 (see code written below).

His argument for sticking with log( 1 + exp(x) ) is that its derivative is much more manageable numerically (the derivative is the logistic function). When the Jacobian, we have to be careful about issues around the derivative being equal to zero, which Michael mentions is an issue here. There's also a bit of literature on log( 1 + exp(x) ); maybe additional reasons why the optimization community likes it can be found there.

The two functions, written in R:

f <- function(x) {
if (x < -10) {
return(exp(x))
} else if (x > 35) {
return(x)
} else {
return(log(1 + exp(x)))
}
}
g <- function(y) {
if (y > 10) {
return(y)
} else {
return(log(exp(y) - 1))
}
}
print( g(f( 1e20 )) )
print( g(f( -740 )) )

Dustin

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: positive transformation
parts:
This summer, I looked into updating our transform code. I think there are HUGE gains to be made in speed and numeric stability.

For the univariate transforms, I had started building out a testing framework that would test values mapped to/from the unconstrained/constrained space between our default initial range, -2 to 2. I looked for a few things (I don't remember all the stuff I looked at), but some of the transforms can't even map that range (on the unconstrained scale) to the constrained scale and back.

If anyone has time and wants to fix it in Stan proper, I can dig up that branch. It's in the math library.


Daniel

messages.subject: Different estimates with xHMC vs. NUTS (was: positive transformation)
parts:
On Tuesday, February 9, 2016 at 4:33:15 AM UTC-5, Michael Betancourt wrote:
The cusp in the Jacobian at y = 0 will cause all kinds of problems for HMC.
But in general the pathological behavior for small x is not necessarily any
better than the overflow for exp, so which is better depends on the context.
Given the cusp in this one, though, I would recommend exp with an effort
to standardize the model as much as possible.

On Feb 9, 2016, at 5:38 AM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:

I think this came up before, but I can't remember what was said. For a transformation of an unbounded parameter (x) to a positive parameter (y), we are using y = exp(x). Would it be better to do something like y = 0.5 * (sqrt(x^2 + 4) + x) whose inverse is x = y - 1 / y? This transformation does not overflow / underflow as rapidly as the exponential one. You can roundtrip negative 1 million and get back -999992.4 and can roundtrip pretty much any big positive number. There could be some numerical difficulties if a user initializes y to a really small number like 1e-9, but that seems like a lesser problem.

I finally got around to trying this transformation:

parameters {
  real x;
}
transformed parameters {
  real<lower=0> y;
  y <- 0.5 * (sqrt(square(x) + 4) + x);
}
model {
  increment_log_prob(log1p(x / sqrt(square(x) + 4))); // Jacobian
  increment_log_prob(gamma_log(y, 3, 1));
}

If you bound y away from zero and use 2.9.x, then it works fine in this case:

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Different estimates with xHMC vs. NUTS (was: positive transformation)
parts:
On Wednesday, July 6, 2016 at 6:02:55 AM UTC-4, Michael Betancourt wrote:
I took a deep look and I believe that it’s an adaptation issue due to
the particularly nasty geometry of this transformation.

But a gamma(3,1) rarely gets very close to zero. It has about a 2e-5 chance of being below 0.05 but in that case x is about -20 and the Jacobian is about -5.3. I suppose during adaptation it might wander closer to zero but the same thing happens if you change y to be a gamma(30,1). Also, if you change y to a gamma(30,1) and restrict x to be positive, then y is still biased but in the other direction. So, I don't think this is a complete explanation as to why NUTS was fine but xHMC is not.

Ben

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Different estimates with xHMC vs. NUTS (was: positive transformation)
parts:
The new code is not XHMC — it’s a slightly modification of the NUTS
algorithm that, if anything, makes things more consistent with the
original implementation.

Again, the transformed density is sufficiently nasty that we know our
typical theoretical guarantees fall apart.  The energy diagnostic does
hint at this, but in only one dimension it’s a noisy diagnostic and hence
it doesn’t come across as strongly as we might like.

This isn’t an issue with light tails that cause divergences, isn’t an issue
with heavy tails that are much, much harder to diagnose in general.

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Different estimates with xHMC vs. NUTS (was: positive transformation)
parts:
It’s heavy tailed!  Even though it mostly avoids negative values
every now and then it will have to sojourn out into negative values
to get the right expectations.  If the sampler cannot get sufficiently
out in the tails then the expectation estimators will be biased.  You
can see the sojourns in the trace plot of x.

I spent some time on the plane looking at some chains with many
iterations and things are perhaps a bit weirder still.  2.9.0 is slightly
high in the 5% quantile of x where as 2.10.0 with the fixed step size
is slightly low, but both are consistent with the true value (~0.82).
Still, the histogram for y with the fixed step size in 2.10.0 and 2.9.0
aren’t consistent and I’m guessing the lower quantiles will be even
more different (although it’ll be hard to decouple that from noise).

If this is a heavy-tail issue then it’s going to be really hard to
investigate as noisy estimators will be a generic problem.
